Concrete Slabs · Lakewood Ranch, FL

Concrete Slabs for Sheds, AC Pads and Parking in Lakewood Ranch

Pricing a slab for a shed, an AC pad or a parking pad in Lakewood Ranch starts at $4–$10 per sq ft installed, current as of October 2026. Manatee County's no-permit list draws a specific line between a small detached deck and a slab poured with footers, which is the first thing worth checking before pricing a pad.

By the Opera Concrete & Pavers estimating team · Updated October 1, 2026

What Manatee's no-permit list actually exempts

A detached deck under 30 inches high and under 120 square feet is exempt from a building permit on the county's current no-permit list, while every attached deck needs one, and a concrete slab poured with footers requires a permit regardless of size (Manatee County, What Does Not Require a Permit). A plain slab-on-grade for a shed or an AC pad, without footers, is the kind of scope that falls closer to the exempt side of that line, though confirming the specific footprint against the current list is worth a call before concrete is ordered.

Reinforcement Placed Where the Load Actually Sits

A slab built for general storage or light foot traffic gets the same baseline reinforcement, wire mesh or dispersed synthetic fiber, as any other flatwork, placed through the slab to hold a crack together rather than to stop one from forming. A pad built specifically for a boat trailer or an RV in Lakewood Ranch sees its heaviest, most repetitive load along two narrow wheel paths rather than spread evenly, worth flagging to whoever is designing the reinforcement and the thickness together, since a slab reinforced for even loading does not automatically perform the same way under two tire lines carrying most of the weight. The mesh or fiber choice works the same either way; what changes is where that reinforcement matters most.

A shed slab, worked out in square feet

Say a homeowner pours an 8 by 10 foot shed slab, 80 square feet, on the side yard of a home built around 2016. At $4–$10 per sq ft installed, that runs $320 to $800, or roughly $480 to $640 at the typical $6–$8 rate, a 4-inch pour over a base compacted in advance. Because the slab is a plain pad without footers and under the county's detached-structure size threshold, it's a candidate for the no-permit exemption, though the final check against the current list and against any CDD drainage easement along that side of the lot still happens before the forms go up.

New-build lots still need a slab sized to current equipment

Because most Lakewood Ranch homes date to the 2010s, the original builder AC pad was sized for equipment that's often smaller than a current replacement heat pump, so a slab swap is as much a resizing job as a repour. A shed slab on a lake or golf-course lot also gets checked against where the CDD maintains drainage along that property line before the pad's location is finalized.

A Garage Addition Slab Isn't the Same Permit Case as a Shed Pad

Structural concrete, the kind that becomes part of a building rather than sitting under a freestanding accessory structure, falls under Florida's state-certified structural masonry specialty contractor scope, which covers foundations, slabs, footers and walls. A detached shed pad in Lakewood Ranch and a slab poured as part of a garage addition tied into the house can look similar from a distance, but the addition slab is far more likely to need a permit and sign-off that a simple accessory pad would not. Assuming both pours qualify for the same lighter paperwork path because they are both just a slab is how a structural job ends up started without the review it actually needed.

A Vapor Retarder Isn't Automatic Under an Unheated Shed

Florida's residential code calls for a 6-mil polyethylene vapor retarder under most slabs on the ground, lapped at least 6 inches at the seams, but the code carves out exceptions for garages and unheated accessory structures. A simple storage shed pad in Lakewood Ranch that will never be conditioned space can often skip the retarder under that exception, while a garage addition meant to become finished, heated living area later does not get the same pass. Knowing which category a structure falls into before the pour, not after, is worth confirming with whoever pulls the permit, since adding a retarder once the slab is poured is not something that can be fixed later.

Clearing an Old Pad in a Tight Backyard Takes Longer Than It Looks

Replacing an old, cracked shed or carport slab starts with breaking it up and hauling the pieces out, and in a backyard without direct truck access that debris often has to be carried or wheeled out the same route the new concrete will eventually come in through. On a Lakewood Ranch job like this, demolition day usually takes longer than the pour itself, not because the slab is large but because every piece of broken concrete has to travel through the same narrow gate or side yard. Once the old pad is cleared, the subgrade underneath finally becomes visible, which sometimes changes the compaction plan if the soil beneath a decades-old pour turns out softer than expected.

A Crack Under the Wheel Line Means Something Different Than One Elsewhere

On a pad that regularly carries a boat trailer or an RV, a crack that lines up with where the wheels or the tongue jack sit is worth more attention than ordinary shrinkage cracking running along a control joint somewhere else on the same Lakewood Ranch pad, since the first is tied to a repeated point load and the second usually is not. Noticing where on the slab a crack actually sits, not just that one exists, helps tell a cosmetic shrinkage crack from an early sign the pad is undersized for what is parked on it. Catching the second kind early is what makes repair, rather than replacement, still an option.

Frequently asked questions

Does a small shed slab need a permit in Lakewood Ranch?

On the Manatee side, a detached deck or structure under 30 inches high and under 120 square feet is exempt from the county's no-permit list, while a concrete slab poured with footers needs a permit regardless of size. Confirm the specific footprint against the current list first.

Can I pour a bigger AC pad than the original builder slab?

Yes, and it's common on homes from the mid-2010s, since current equipment often needs a larger footprint than the original unit. The new pad's size is checked against the no-permit threshold the same as any other slab.

Does a shed slab on a lake lot need extra checks?

Often, since the CDD maintains drainage along some lake-facing property lines. We confirm the shed's placement against any drainage easement before pricing the slab on a lot like that.
